title: Amy Carmichael
hookLine: in south India, a missionary opens her home to girls at risk of exploitation and writes of love that costs

cards: Early one morning, a little girl stands at the door of a mission house in south India. She has run away in the night.
The story told about her, by the woman who opened the door, is that she had been given to a temple as a small child, and she was afraid of what was coming. Her name, in that story, is Preena.
The woman at the door is Amy Carmichael, a missionary from Ireland who wears a sari and works alongside Indian women. She takes the child in. The people who claim the girl come to get her back.

teach.b: Through that child and others, Carmichael learned of a custom in parts of India by which some girls were given to temples as children, and some were sexually exploited as they grew. She wasn't the only one to oppose it.
Indian reformers, Hindu and Christian, campaigned against the practice too, and Indian law later banned it.
Carmichael's part was a home. It grew into a large household at a place called Dohnavur, later including boys as well. The children called her Amma, mother.
Indian coworkers ran much of it beside her. She wanted it to be a family, not an institution. That home had a price.

teach.h: THE COST OF TAKING THEM IN.
teach.b: Taking children in made her enemies and brought her trouble. She gave up comfort, home leave, and a life anyone in Ireland would have recognized.
In her poems and books she wrote about love that costs: love that gives up nothing, she said, isn't really love.

The first letter of John says something close, in the King James Bible: "My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth." Deed and truth: love you can see by what it gives up.

Looking back, some Christians remember her with deep gratitude, and some also ask hard questions about the mission era she worked in. Neither takes away the girl at the door, or the door that stayed open.

how: Amy Carmichael's books are read for devotion by some Christians, and the household she founded at Dohnavur continues as a community led by Indian Christians.

games.q: a girl who ran away in the night stands at your door. the people who claim her want her back. what do you do?
o: send her back. it isn't your business.
take her in and protect her, whatever it costs.
ask her to wait outside while you think.
games.why: Carmichael took her in and didn't hand her over. the household at Dohnavur grew from that door.

practice: Bring to mind a child in your life, your own, a niece, a neighbor's kid, a student, and ask quietly: is there one thing I could do to make this child safer, or to be an adult they could tell if something were wrong?

Maybe closer attention, or simply being someone steady; if you're ever worried a child is in danger, the protecting step is to call the people whose job it is. If you pray, hold that child before God by name.

wordCard.voice: Amy Carmichael. A missionary in south India who opened her home to girls at risk, and became Amma to a household of children.
